Five Cu–Cr–Zr alloy powders were fabricated from five different master alloys, which in turn were produced by vacuum induction melting.
A 5 kg laboratory water atomiser (Atomising Systems Ltd, RD 106) was employed to produce the powders.

Powder preforms from powders 1, 3 and 4, with a density of 85% of the theoretical value, were inverse extruded in a 200 ton press at 250 and 300 uC respectively; the preforms were heated up in a tube furnace under an Ar–5%H2 atmosphere before placed in the extrusion rig.

Powder 3 contained a second phase, distributed throughout the matrix, which was identified as elemental chromium by EDS analysis.
the only possible second phases that should be present at room temperature are Cr and a Cu–Zr intermetallic, which in other studies on Cu–Cr–Zr alloys has been identified as Cu5Zr.
Evidence of internal Cr2O3 particles was found in consolidated samples in the as extruded condition, suggesting that they were incorporated into the alloy during air melting.
The microstructure of the Cu–Cr–Zr powder batches was mainly characterised by equiaxed cells having mean sizes in the range 2–5 mm

The material had a fine equiaxed subgrain structure and no evidence of fine precipitation within the subgrains was found at this stage. A subgrain size of 197 nm was measured by image analysis from a total of 130 cells.

Figure 6 also shows the presence of intense black dot type precipitation resulting from the decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution due to aging. An approximate size distribution of these fine precipitates was calculated by measuring the strain field they produced in the material. This field is represented by the black contrast zone surrounding each precipitate observed under a double beam condition. A mean size of 4.2 nm was calculated from a total of 200 particles measured.

The microstructure consisted of fine highly poligonised subgrains, some of them revealing fine black dot type precipitation, as indicated by point ‘A’, similar to that already found in samples consolidated by inverse extrusion in the aged condition. As for inverse extruded samples, rounded dark particles were found distributed throughout the microstructure (point ‘B’); such particles were constituted of chromium and oxygen, as indicated by EDS analysis. The mean subgrain size measured was 600 nm; this value was larger than the value determined for samples consolidated by inverse warm extrusion in the aged condition.

Few dislocations, smooth subgrain boundaries and twins were also observed in the microstructure suggesting the occurrence of recrystallisation in the alloy.
The maximum hardness measured in samples based on powders 1 and 4 were 174 and 269 VHN respectively.
The largest peak hardness measured in the extruded alloys (295 VHN) was found in the sample based on powder 3 aged for 1.5 h.
A poor response to aging was observed in alloy T1 as a maximum hardness of 153 VHN was achieved on aging, that value being similar to the hardness measured in the ‘as conformed’ condition (152 VHN).
